summary: Reviews motivations for internationalized top level domain names, especially for countries whose main language is not written in a Roman script, and suggestions made to provide them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: People who write in other alphabets want web addresses endings in their own letters. This memo looks at why and at ideas for making it work.

questions: how can people type domain names in their own language
what is internationalization for domain names
subtitle: Letting people in other countries type domain names in their own alphabets.

tldr.problem: People who do not write in Roman characters want domain names in their own scripts, but the DNS requires ASCII. Modifying DNS itself is difficult and slow. How can non-Roman-speaking users type domain names in their own languages?
tldr.mechanism: Instead of changing DNS, applications can maintain local translation tables that map native-language TLD names (like a country name in Arabic) to the standard ASCII TLD (like a country code). When a user types a local name, the application translates it to ASCII before querying DNS.
tldr.outcome: This client-side approach avoids changing DNS infrastructure, lets every TLD appear in every language, and scales better than creating new internationalized TLDs. However, it requires user awareness that locally-translated names are presentation-only.

today: RFC 4185 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It proposes a localization approach as an alternative or supplement to IDNA-based internationalization. The RFC community has continued to develop IDNA and internationalized domain names, though the client-side translation table approach described here remains an option for implementations.

sections.title: The Problem of International Domain Names
sections.content: The Domain Name System was designed for ASCII characters. All top-level domains (TLDs) today use ASCII, usually following the letter-digit-hyphen rules. Users who write in Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, or other non-Roman scripts are forced to type domain names in ASCII or use systems like IDNA that convert their input to a special encoded form. A more user-friendly approach would let them type entire domain names in their native script. The challenge is that the DNS cannot be easily changed to support non-ASCII characters globally, so any solution must work with the existing DNS infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book (DNS) only speaks English. People in other countries want to look things up in their own words, not English ones.

sections.title: Why Focus on TLDs Only
sections.content: Modifying the entire DNS to accept non-ASCII names everywhere would be extremely disruptive and slow to deploy. However, TLDs are special: they are at the root of the namespace, are limited in number, and their administration is centralized. This makes them a natural place to focus a localization effort. A solution that works for TLDs (like letting a Korean user see .kr as a Korean name) could be applied without changing the DNS protocol itself, using only application-level translation tables.
sections.plainLanguage: You could translate every page on the internet, but that is too much work. Just translating the top-level domain part is simpler and covers what people care about most.

sections.title: Local Translation Tables for TLDs
sections.content:
Applications like web browsers would maintain a table mapping native-language TLD names to their standard ASCII forms. For a country code TLD, the local name might be the country's name written in its own script. For generic TLDs, the local name might be a translation of the function (e.g., « commercial » in French instead of « .com »). When a user types a domain name, the browser's TLD mapper translates the local name to ASCII before processing it. When displaying a domain name received from elsewhere, the mapper translates it to local form for the user to read.

This approach is compatible with IDNA (Internationalized Domain Names in Applications), which already requires applications to do transformation work for the second and lower levels. The additional translation of TLDs fits naturally into existing client-side processing.
sections.plainLanguage: A browser could keep a little table saying « when someone types Russian for 'China', turn that into 'cn' ». The rest of the name is handled normally.

sections.title: Benefits of This Approach
sections.content: Every TLD can be represented in every language and script, without requiring new TLDs to be created. Countries with multiple languages do not need multiple domains. Administrative complexity is minimal: each locale maintains its own translation table, with no need for global coordination. The approach works immediately with existing DNS and does not require the lengthy deployment time that protocol changes would demand. In principle, translations could even differ from one region to another, as long as users understand that international interchange still requires ASCII TLD names. Users who need to share domain names across language boundaries can exchange the standard ASCII forms.
sections.plainLanguage: A Korean user sees everything in Korean, a Japanese user sees everything in Japanese, and they both mean the same thing when they say the code for their respective countries.

sections.title: Costs and Constraints
sections.content: This solution places some burden on users: they must understand that local translations are a presentation feature and that the actual DNS names are in ASCII. When sending domain names to others or storing them durably, the ASCII form is required. If applications on the same system use different translation tables, users might become confused. Additionally, if many new TLDs are added frequently, maintaining translation tables in every application and on every client machine would become burdensome. These tables do not provide true internationalization for sub-domains (only the top level), and applications must coordinate or warn users when local names differ from system to system.
sections.plainLanguage: Users have to remember that under the hood, the computer is still speaking English to the DNS. If they cut and paste a translated name into an email, the recipient might not understand it. And keeping translation tables up-to-date is work.

sections.title: Security and Reliability
sections.content: Since local translations are a presentation layer, they should never be used in security-sensitive contexts like certificate names, access control lists, or configuration files, where the actual ASCII name must be verified. Translation tables should be protected from tampering, especially if they are downloaded from a server. Client applications should ensure that translation tables are used consistently, and where they differ across systems, users should be made aware of this. The approach relies on user awareness of the difference between local presentation forms and the actual DNS names required for interchange.
sections.plainLanguage: When something really matters, like a security certificate, you should use the real DNS name, not the translated one. Make sure no one can sneak bad translations into your software.
